English: PUBLIC NOTICE15th Jul 2026. The Commission reminds all voters that taking photographs or recording images of marked ballot papers inside the polling booth is strictly prohibited and constitutes an election offence under Section 7(3)(e) of the Election Offences Act, No. 37 of 2016. Section 7(3)(e) of the Election Offences Act states that a person attending any proceedings relating to an election who, without lawful excuse, captures an image of any marked ballot for purposes of financial gain or for showing allegiance, commits an offence. The offence is punishable by a fine not exceeding KSh 1 million, or imprisonment for a term not exceeding three years, or both. The Commission urges all voters to comply with this legal requirement in order to protect the secrecy and integrity of the ballot. For accurate and up-to-date information, please visit our official website (https://iebc.or.ke) and follow our verified social media platforms (@IEBCKenya). #16thJulyByElection #YourVoteYourVoice #TalkWithIEBC #StopFakeNews

English: Press Release - Update on Preparedness for the 16th July 2026 Ol Kalou By-Election14th Jul 2026. The Commission wishes to inform the nation that all preparations for the by-election scheduled for Thursday, 16th July 2026, to fill the position of Member of National Assembly for Ol Kalou Constituency in Nyandarua County are progressing as planned. All registered voters in Ol Kalou Constituency MUST present their national identity card or valid passport on polling day, as these remain the primary identification documents required for voting. The Register of Voters for the Ol Kalou Constituency by-election remains secure. Claims that the Register has been manipulated are false, misleading and unsupported by evidence. The Commission condemns such misleading claims and urges all stakeholders to refrain from spreading misinformation and disinformation. Polling stations will open at 6:00 a.m. and close at 5:00 p.m. Where polling commences later than scheduled due to unforeseen circumstances, the lost time will be compensated to ensure that voters receive the full polling period. All voters who are in the queue by 5:00 p.m. will be allowed to cast their ballots. Taking photographs or recording images of marked ballot papers inside the polling booth is strictly prohibited and constitutes an election offence under Section 7(3)(e) of the Election Offences Act, No. 37 of 2016. The Commission, in close collaboration with the National Police Service, has put in place adequate security arrangements to ensure a peaceful and orderly electoral process. Two uniformed police officers will be deployed at every polling station, while additional officers will be stationed at tallying centres to maintain law and order and safeguard the integrity of the election. All political parties, candidates, agents and supporters are reminded that compliance with the Electoral Code of Conduct is mandatory. The Commission will not hesitate to invoke all enforcement measures provided for under the Electoral Code of Conduct without fear or favour. The Commission's investigation team is actively investigating all alleged violations with a view to fully enforcing the Code. The Commission calls upon voters, political parties, candidates, observers, civil society organizations and members of the public to report any electoral offence or breach of the Electoral Code of Conduct. Members of the public are encouraged to REPORT and PROVIDE evidence of any electoral malpractice to the Commission, the National Police Service or any other authorized investigative agency. The Commission remains steadfast in its commitment to delivering a peaceful, free, fair, transparent and credible election whose outcome reflects the freely expressed will of the people. Registered voters of Ol Kalou Constituency: Your vote is your voice. Turn out in large numbers, cast your ballot and peacefully shape the future of your constituency. English: IEBC Participates in Regional EMB Capacity-Building and Experience-Sharing Programme11th Jun 2026. The Independent Electoral and Boundaries Commission (IEBC) is participating in a regional Electoral Management Bodies (EMBs) Capacity-Building and Experience-Sharing Programme taking place in Machakos, Kenya, from 10 to 13 June 2026. The programme, organized under the auspices of the Common Market for Eastern and Southern Africa (COMESA) with technical support from the Electoral Institute for Sustainable Democracy in Africa (EISA), brings together Commissioners and senior electoral officials from Kenya, Seychelles, Malawi, and Uganda to strengthen electoral governance and promote peer learning across the region. The engagement provides a platform for electoral leaders to exchange experiences, share best practices, and discuss emerging challenges affecting election administration in Africa. The discussions focus on strengthening institutional independence, enhancing leadership and decision-making capacities, promoting electoral integrity, and improving stakeholder engagement. A key feature of the programme is the examination of contemporary challenges facing electoral management bodies, including misinformation and disinformation, the growing influence of artificial intelligence and digital technologies in electoral processes, crisis communication, and electoral dispute resolution mechanisms. Speaking during the programme on behalf of the Chairperson, Commissioner Dr. Alutalala Mukhwana welcomed the programme and termed it timely and enriching. “We have the talent, technology, and we have the patriotic duty to deliver for our people,” said Dr. Alutalala as he officially opened the three-day programme. Dr. Alutalala further emphasized the importance of regional collaboration and knowledge sharing in building resilient electoral institutions capable of delivering credible, transparent, and inclusive elections. Through interactive sessions, expert presentations, case studies, and peer-to-peer learning, participants are exploring practical approaches to addressing common electoral challenges while identifying innovative solutions that can enhance public confidence in electoral processes. The participation of the IEBC underscores the Commission's commitment to continuous institutional learning, professional development, and the adoption of regional best practices that contribute to the effective management of elections and strengthening democracy in Kenya. #16thJulyByelection #KuraYakoSautiYako #IEBCStrategicPlan #IEBCEOP

English: IEBC, UNDP Collaborate to Enhance Electoral Integrity and Preparedness for 20279th Jun 2026. The Commission, led by Chairperson Erastus Ethekon, today attended a meeting of the local Project Appraisal Committee (LPAC) of the UNDP-led Elections Project document to finalise plans for the Elections Basket Fund project ahead of the 2027 General Election. Speaking during the meeting, Ethekon thanked the development partners, security agencies, gender, youth and women groups present for their support and noted that an election is not a one-day event but a journey where agencies walk together to help achieve an inclusive, transparent, credible, free and fair election. "This collaboration is important for us to build trust and legitimacy of the electoral processes. It is the framework to support elections and a vehicle to mobilise resources for both technical and financial support in the build-up to the 2027 General Election," said Ethekon. The Elections Project document defines the scope, outcomes, outputs and activities required to be implemented prior to the 2027 General Election. If approved and implemented, it will enhance stakeholder engagement and strengthen efforts towards delivering a transparent and credible election. "Election is a journey and I call upon everyone present here today to act responsibly, be accountable for the resources available and work together to achieve tangible results. This document will be taken to the Attorney General and National Treasury for approval before we sign and implement it. I will follow up on the remaining processes to ensure that it is cleared and approved," said Ethekon. Commissioner Ann Nderitu, CBS, said the Elections Project document is anchored on five priorities arising from the 2025 Needs Assessment Mission, including: participation of youth, women and people living with disabilities; strengthening stakeholder engagement and communication; capacity building and technical assistance; electoral security, preparation and early risk awareness coordination; and information integrity to counter misinformation, disinformation and online harm. UNDP’s Resident Representative Jean-Luc Stalon reiterated their support in ensuring the Commission delivers on its constitutional mandate. UNDP has played a pivotal role over successive elections in supporting Kenya to deepen its democracy by contributing to institutional capacity and electoral integrity. LPAC is a mandatory review mechanism where key national partners and concerned UN agencies formally evaluate the project's design, budget availability and technical alignment. The expected outcome is a formal endorsement of the project document before submission to the Office of the Attorney General and National Treasury for approval. #16thJulyByelection #KuraYakoSautiYako #IEBCStrategicPlan #IEBCEOP

English: IEBC Engages MSMEs and Boda Boda Associations on Voter Education Ahead of 2027 General Election29th May 2026. Today, IEBC, led by Deputy Commission Secretary – Operations, Ruth Kulundu, met with representatives from the Biashara Ndogo Association of Kenya and the BodaBoda Association of Kenya to explore collaboration opportunities on voter education ahead of the 2027 General Election. Speaking during the meeting, Kulundu recognized the critical role MSMEs play in Kenya’s economy and applauded the Associations for proactively seeking partnership with IEBC in strengthening civic and voter education across the country. She noted that the extensive grassroots networks of small businesses and the boda boda sector present a unique opportunity for the Commission to expand the reach of voter education messages and deepen public understanding of electoral processes. The proposed collaboration, which will be formalized through a Memorandum of Understanding (MoU), is expected to support dissemination of voter education information, enhance voter registration outreach, and promote peaceful participation in the electoral process. Kulundu further emphasized that boda boda riders can play a transformative role as ambassadors of peace during the electioneering period, helping to foster national cohesion and responsible civic engagement ahead of the 2027 General Election. Marcos Mwangi, Chairman of the Biashara Ndogo Association of Kenya, affirmed that the Association is non-partisan and committed to empowering its members through voter education and access to voter registration services at the grassroots level. English: IEBC Commissioner Dr. Alutalala Joins African Dialogue on Election Observer Accreditation12th May 2026. Today, IEBC Commissioner Dr. Alutalala Mukhwana, Chairperson of the Voter Education, Partnerships, Communication and Stakeholder Engagement Committee, attended a Joint Dialogue on Citizen Election Observer Accreditation in Africa. The event brought together senior electoral commissioners and directors from Election Management Bodies (EMBs) in Ghana, Malawi, the Democratic Republic of Congo, South Africa, Nigeria, and Kenya to discuss strengthening accreditation frameworks for citizen election observers across the continent. While opening the roundtable discussion, Dr. Mukhwana noted that elections in Africa attract enormous public interest and expectation. He emphasized that election observation is no longer a ceremonial addition to the democratic process, but an integral part of electoral integrity. He added that the presence of observers helps simplify and communicate complex electoral processes to the public, thereby enhancing transparency, accountability, and trust in electoral administration. He further observed that EMBs and observer groups continue to face challenges such as administrative friction, scalability, and technological changes. He stated that IEBC is currently undertaking efforts to modernize its accreditation management systems, adding that such dialogues provide an important platform for progressive solutions and institutional reform. Dr. Alutalala underscored that despite differing national experiences, the shared objective remains the establishment of a gold standard for accreditation that balances the integrity and security of electoral processes with inclusivity and openness. He concluded by stressing that true democratic fidelity requires grassroots civil society organizations, community networks, and observer groups to have a place at the national democratic table. Mr. Richard Klein, Global Director for Elections at the National Democratic Institute (NDI), noted that EMBs and non-partisan citizen election observers have both built significant capacity over the past four decades in promoting credible elections. He added that while accreditation is intended to support transparent, participatory, and accountable elections, global trends show that the process is becoming increasingly complex, creating challenges for both EMBs and observer groups. The event serves as a platform for constructive networking and engagement between EMBs and citizen observer groups, reaffirming non-partisan citizen observation as a cornerstone of transparent and accountable elections across Africa

English: IEBC Commissioner Dr. Ann Nderitu, CBS Calls for Public Trust and Institutional Strengthening at ICS Conference25th Apr 2026. IEBC Commissioner Dr. Ann Nderitu, CBS attended the Institute of Certified Secretaries (ICS) 30th Annual International Conference in Mombasa, themed “Resilient Governance for Thriving Economies.” Commissioner Dr. Ann took part in a panel discussion on rebuilding public trust in electoral institutions, alongside JLAC’s Chairperson Hon. George Gitonga Murugara, CBS (MP for Tharaka Constituency), Senior Counsel Charles Kanjama, President of the Law Society of Kenya (LSK), and Amb. FCS Dr. Koki Muli Grignon. Dr. Ann likened the electoral process to the role of a midwife, explaining that just as a midwife ensures the safe delivery of a child without determining the gender, the Commission facilitates the electoral process without influencing the outcome. This, she noted, underscores the Commission's commitment to delivering a transparent, credible, free, fair and inclusive electoral process. She highlighted the importance of shared responsibility in protecting electoral institutions. While public scrutiny is necessary, sustained attacks on institutions can weaken public confidence and hinder their effectiveness. She urged Kenyans to foster patience and trust in institutional processes while continuing to demand accountability. Dr. Ann also stressed the need to strengthen institutional capacity through continuous staff training, adequate resourcing and proper management of the Register of Voters (RoV) and election materials. She added that sufficient funding is critical, as elections are resource-intensive and require proper financial support to ensure effective implementation. She concluded by underscoring that credible elections depend on collaboration among all electoral stakeholders, including the government, the electoral body, voters, citizens, inter alia. She noted that such collaboration would ensure that IEBC delivers transparent, inclusive, free, fair elections, which are key to building public trust and strengthening democracy. #ECVR2026 #YourVoteYourFuture #14thMayByelections #TalkWithIEBC #StopFakeNews

English: IEBC Chairperson Leads CSR and Stakeholder Engagement in Turkana During ECVR25th Apr 2026. The Independent Electoral and Boundaries Commission(IEBC) Chairperson Erastus Ethekon together with Kenya Literature Bureau (KLB) Managing Director George Wanga, jointly undertook a Corporate Social Responsibility (CSR) by distributing textbooks, stationery and footballs to several schools that converged at RCEA Secondary School in Lokori, Turkana East Constituency during quality assurance and oversight of the Enhanced Continuous Voter Registration (ECVR). The Commission also held a stakeholder engagement forum and met with local youth groups, women groups, elders, marginalized communities, PWDs, CBO, religious leaders and Turkana Professional Association. The locals voiced their challenges in accessing voter registration centers owing to poor road network and insecurity. “We are here to listen to all Kenyans and your petitions will be reviewed and acted upon. IEBC’s verification portal is accurate and working and any voter can verify their details in the system using their mobile phones or online,” said Ethekon. The Chairperson said that the Commission had agreed not to stay in office, but to visit each part of the country to oversee the registration of voters and engage stakeholders including the national government to enhance issuance of national Identity Cards to make all Kenyans participate in the electoral process and have a legitimate and transparent 2027 General Election. Locals leaders shared challenges affecting Turkana County such as accessibility of registration centers, insecurity, boundaries and inclusion. However, the Chaiperson observed that without the required population number, there cannot be as many wards as communities want “Distribution of national resources requires numbers, even at county level the distribution is based on population,” he said. Ethekon urged Kenyans to come out register and be counted. He also called upon religious leaders to take the registration exercise seriously and ask their congregants to embrace the exercise. The Chairperson also took the opportunity to meet IEBCTurkana County staff led by County Elections Manager Amos Obonyo, who voiced their challenges and concerns in implementating #ECVR2026. Turkana county is among the top ten counties leading in new voter registration in the ongoing ECVR. Ethekon lauded the efforts put in place by the IEBC staff, the local leadership and all stakeholders in Turkana County to ensure ECVR is a success. The Commission targets to register over 2.5 million new voters during the ECVR, which ends on 28th April 2026. Thereafter, the Continuous Voter Registration (CVR) will resume at the 57 Huduma centres, @IEBCKenya 290 constituencies across the country and Customer Experience Center at Anniversary Towers. Turkana East MP Nicholas Nixon Ngikolong, who handed a memorandum/petition to the chairperson, highlighted the challenges the constituents are enduring in a bid to access registration as voters under the ongoing ECVR exercise. The vast constituency covers roughly 70,000 square kilometres. #ECVR2026 #YourVoteYourFuture #14thMayByelections #TalkWithIEBC #StopFakeNews

English: IEBC Vice Chairperson Rallies Kilifi Stakeholders as Voter Registration Deadline Nears16th Apr 2026. With 12 days remaining before the conclusion of the Enhanced Continuous Voter Registration (ECVR) exercise, IEBC Vice Chairperson Fahima Araphat Abdallah, OGW, led Kilifi County stakeholder engagement forum aimed at strengthening voter registration efforts. The forum seeks to gather input and support from various stakeholders while encouraging eligible residents to register before the deadline on Thursday 28th April 2026. The engagement brought together representatives from government, civil society, the private sector, and community leadership to discuss practical strategies for increasing voter turnout. Discussions focused on addressing barriers to registration and enhancing collaboration to ensure more eligible citizens are reached within the remaining period. The Vice Chairperson noted that the Commission launched the exercise on 30th March to bring services closer to the people. Over 12,000 clerks, largely youth, were deployed across wards nationwide, with some conducting door to door registration to ensure inclusivity, particularly for persons with disabilities and other underserved groups. She emphasized that there will be no extension beyond 28th April 2026 due to budgetary constraints and urged eligible citizens to take advantage of the remaining days. After the deadline, registration services will continue at constituency offices, Huduma Centres, and the IEBC Customer Experience Centre at Anniversary Towers. She also reminded citizens that only a national ID or valid passport is required to vote not the acknowledge slip. The Vice Chairperson commended the national government for providing security during the exercise and stressed the importance of maintaining peace and stability. She called on all stakeholders to work together in safeguarding the country’s stability and to act as ambassadors in mobilizing more citizens to register. During the forum, Acting County Elections Manager Jumaa Musa Jumaa outlined strategies to enhance voter registration in Kilifi County, emphasizing the importance of a credible voter register and community based approaches. Kilifi North Deputy County Commissioner Samuel Mutisya also appreciated the initiative, noting ongoing mobilization efforts but highlighting delays in national ID issuance as a key challenge, and calling for expedited processing to improve registration outcomes. #ECVR2026 #YourVoteYourFuture #14thMayByelections #TalkWithIEBC #StopFakeNews

English: Commissioner Dr. Ann Nderitu CBS Calls for Gender-Responsive Electoral Processes at Legislative Summit16th Apr 2026. Independent Electoral and Boundaries Commission(IEBC) , represented by Commissioner Dr. Ann Nderitu, CBS, is participating in the 6th County Assemblies Legislative Summit themed “Resilient County Assemblies: Reinforcing Representation, Legislation, and Oversight,” from 13th to 17th April 2026 in Mombasa County. The Summit, convened by the County Assemblies Forum (CAF), brought together stakeholders to strengthen legislative, representation, and oversight capacities across Kenya’s 47 County Assemblies. Presenting during General Session V on fair and inclusive elections, Commissioner Ann emphasized the need for gender-responsive planning, preparedness, and risk management in electoral processes. She noted that although women form a larger share of the population and often record higher voter turnout, they remain underrepresented in the voter register and elective positions. She called for continuous review of the register to ensure inclusivity. The Commissioner identified key barriers to women’s participation, including limited access to timely electoral information, financial constraints, and persistent societal biases. Many women, she observed, receive election information late due to competing responsibilities, underscoring the need for targeted civic and voter education. Commissioner Ann also raised concern over gender-based electoral violence, including cyberbullying and online harassment, which continue to discourage women from seeking leadership. She called for stronger measures to ensure safety and a level playing field. In conclusion, she emphasized that inclusive elections require collective action, calling on all stakeholders including men to support women’s participation and leadership in electoral processes. She also urged political parties to be more intentional in supporting women candidates through fair nomination processes and equitable placement. #ECVR2026 #YourVoteYourFuture #14thMayByelections #TalkWithIEBC #StopFakeNews

English: IEBC Intensifies Stakeholder Engagement to Boost Voter Registration in Busia14th Apr 2026. As the Enhanced Continuous Voter Registration (ECVR) exercise progresses, Independent Electoral and Boundaries Commission(IEBC) continues to intensify stakeholder engagement across the country to ensure that as many eligible Kenyans as possible are registered within the ongoing 30-day exercise ending on 28th April 2026. Led by Commissioner Dr. Alutalala Mukhwana, the Commission today engaged a wide range of stakeholders, including Busia County leadership, County Commissioner, Sub-County administrators, media, representatives of persons with disabilities (PWDs), women, youth, county security teams, the Registrar of Persons, as well as civil society and community representatives. The engagement reaffirmed that credible and inclusive elections are a shared responsibility that extends beyond the Commission. During the discussions, several key issues were raised that are crucial to the success of the ECVR exercise. Stakeholders highlighted the challenge of uncollected national identification cards, noting that many eligible citizens remain unregistered simply because they have not picked up their IDs. To address this, there were strong calls for enhanced collaboration between IEBC, the National Registration Bureau (NRB), National Government Administrative Officers (NGAO), and Nyumba Kumi elders to facilitate the delivery of IDs to their rightful owners, while the Commission simultaneously deploys voter registration kits closer to communities. Dr. Paul Otuoma, Governor of Busia County, pledged full support and continued collaboration with IEBC, both during the ECVR period and beyond. He called upon all county government structures—including CECs and Heads of Departments—to actively mobilize the public, especially the youth, to come out and register. He underscored that elections cannot be left to IEBC alone and urged a multi-stakeholder approach to ensure that no eligible Kenyan with an ID is left out of the process. Stephen Orinde, Busia County Commissioner, pledged to work closely with IEBC offices, sub-county administrators, chiefs, assistant chiefs and village elders to ensure maximum outreach. He also assured the public of adequate security during voter registration and in the lead-up to the General Election, reinforcing confidence in a safe and orderly process. In a strong show of support, NGAO assured the Commission of its commitment to help achieve voter registration targets by mobilizing communities at the grassroots level, learning from high-performing sub-counties, and replicating best practices across the region. Additionally, NGAO reaffirmed its role in ensuring security throughout the exercise, committing to curb any form of goonism or insecurity and to guarantee a peaceful and conducive environment for voter registration. Stakeholders also emphasized the urgent need to address the growing threat of misinformation, disinformation, and mal-information, particularly on social media platforms. There was a collective call for all partners and the public to verify information through official IEBC channels before acting on or sharing it, in order to safeguard the integrity of the electoral process. #ECVR2026 #YourVoteYourFuture #14thMayByelections #TalkWithIEBC #StopFakeNews

English: IEBC Engages Laikipia Stakeholders to Boost Voter Registration and Inclusion14th Apr 2026. Independent Electoral and Boundaries Commission(IEBC) today led by Commissioner Dr. Ann Nderitu CBS, convened a stakeholder engagement meeting in Laikipia County, bringing together stakeholders from all constituencies in Laikipia. While addressing the stakeholders, Commissioner Dr. Ann Nderitu emphasized the importance of inclusive participation in strengthening democratic processes. “We are all here because of one shared goal: to strengthen our country’s democracy. The County Election Manager for Laikipia County, Mr. Obadiah Kariuki, while opening the session, delivered a detailed presentation on the electoral process. He guided participants through the various phases of the electoral cycle, underscoring the critical role of public participation at every stage. He emphasized that the Commission places great importance on stakeholder engagement, recognizing that it cannot work in isolation. These engagements promote inclusivity and enable stakeholders to contribute meaningfully to electoral processes. English: JLAC Convenes Key Institutions to Strengthen 2027 Election Preparedness31st Mar 2026. Today, the Departmental Committee on Justice and Legal Affairs (JLAC) held a joint stakeholder engagement bringing together IEBCK, Judiciary, the Office of the Registrar of Political Parties (ORPP), and the Witness Protection Agency (WPA). The retreat focused on enhancing preparedness for the 2027 General Election (#2027GE) and advancing report writing for the Public Participation Bill, underscoring the importance of collaboration in strengthening Kenya’s democratic processes. In his welcoming remarks, Hon. George Gitonga Murugara, CBS, MP (Tharaka Constituency) and Chairperson of JLAC, reaffirmed the Committee’s unwavering support for the Commission. He emphasized that both he and the entire JLAC membership are committed to working closely with IEBC to ensure the delivery of a free, fair and credible 2027 General Election, in support of Kenya’s democracy. IEBC Chairperson Erastus Ethekon, HSC, highlighted the Commission’s ongoing and upcoming activities aimed at preparing for the 2027 polls. He expressed appreciation to JLAC for its continued support and noted that the Commission has placed significant focus on voter registration through the Enhanced Continuous Voter Registration (ECVR) exercise, which was recently launched in Shimoni, Kwale. The Chairperson also noted the encouraging enthusiasm among young people in participating in the democratic process, with many taking an active role in mobilizing their peers to register as voters. He reaffirmed the Commission’s commitment to strengthening electoral processes and deepening democratic governance. He emphasized the importance of integrity, inclusion and active citizen participation as key pillars in building public trust and ensuring the delivery of credible elections. Commissioner Dr. Ann Nderitu, CBS, Chairperson of the Election Operations Committee, presented the Commission’s roadmap towards the 2027 General Election. Her presentation outlined key areas of focus including administrative preparedness, advancements in electoral technology such as the upgrade of the Kenya Integrated Election Management System (KIEMS), expansion of voter registration both locally and in the diaspora, and intensified voter education and engagement initiatives. Commissioner Prof. Francis O. Adoul, Chairperson of the Research, Innovation and ICT Committee, presented a detailed justification for the disposal of legacy Morpho KIEMS kits. He highlighted that the kits, now approximately ten years old, are facing multiple technical challenges including battery degradation, physical wear and tear, damaged ports, outdated operating systems and discontinued vendor support. The Commission will seek inter-agency collaboration by partnering with agencies like the National Registration Bureau (NRB) to fast-track the issuance of IDs, which are a legal prerequisite for voter registration. The requirement for one to be registered as a voter is that they should be a Kenyan citizen of majority age and with a national identification card or valid passport. English: IEBC, KMSWG Hold Workshop to Review MOU Between IEBC and the Media10th Mar 2026. Today Independent Electoral and Boundaries Commission(IEBC) Dr. Alutalala Mukhwana, Chairperson – Voter Education, Partnerships, Communication & Stakeholder Engagement Committee, brought together the Kenya Media Sector Working Group for a Workshop on Review of the MOU Between IEBC and the Media. Dr. Alutalala opened the workshop by highlighting the importance of a trust-based relationship between the media and IEBC. He noted that the media is critical in helping citizens understand how elections work, and countering dis/misinformation that can overshadow facts. Dr. Alutalala emphasized that restoring public confidence is as crucial as personal integrity and that elections begin long before polling day, “Help the public understand the work we do. Help them see the role of an electoral administrator. The media is essential in rebuilding public confidence in our democratic process,” he said. This MOU is more than a document. It’s a framework for partnership, a tool to empower journalists, and a pathway to a transparent, credible and inclusive election in 2027. Moses Sunkuli, OGW, Ag. Commission Secretary/CEO reflected on lessons from past elections, emphasizing that elections are a continuous process. Journalists must understand every stage—from voter registration and verification to results transmission—to ensure accurate reporting. “As we prepare for the 2027 General Election, this engagement is both timely and necessary. Elections take place within a dynamic information environment where facts, narratives and public trust interact and shape public perception. In that space, the partnership between the electoral management body and the media is indispensable,” he said. Felix Oduor, Executive Director, ELGIA, highlighted the historical role of media in Kenya’s electoral process, noting that collaborative engagement between electoral bodies and the media has precedent both locally and internationally. He emphasized that such partnerships enhance transparency and public trust, citing examples from previous elections and comparative experiences from Ghana and the United States. Felix stressed that while challenges exist, particularly around timing and coordination, a well-structured framework for media engagement can significantly strengthen electoral integrity and ensure that the public receives accurate, timely information. Zubeidah Kananu, President of KEG, emphasized the diversity of the media sector and the responsibility it carries. "Through this MOU, we ensure journalists are trained, informed, and ready to report elections responsibly, minimizing misinformation and conflict,", she noted. Martin Maasai, Trustee at KEG and Chairperson of the Media Freedoms & Ethics Committee, reflected on the current state of the media industry, noting the rapid turnover of experienced journalists and the prevalence of younger reporters covering elections for the first time. He stressed the importance of creating spaces for engagement and training between the media and the IEBC, ensuring journalists understand the full electoral process—from voter registration to the announcement of results. Maasai emphasized that responsible and informed reporting is essential for transparency, public confidence and preventing misinformation, reminding participants that “journalists do what they do precisely because they care about this country.” Victor Bwire, Director of Media Training and Development, MCK, highlighted the collaborative efforts already underway between MCK and IEBC to train journalists on electoral processes and responsible election reporting. He noted the challenges posed by Kenya’s vast media landscape, with hundreds of radio, TV, digital and blog platforms, emphasizing that standardized training and clear guidelines are essential for consistent, accurate coverage. Bwire also spoke on emerging issues like artificial intelligence, digital media, and user-generated content, explaining that the new Code of Ethics and the “Introduction to Media Practice” course aim to equip all media practitioners—including non-journalists—with the skills to report ethically and professionally. He concluded by stressing that coordinated reporting, journalist safety, and adherence to standards are critical for enhancing public trust and credibility in elections. The workshop reinforced the partnership between IEBC and the media, ensuring journalists are equipped to safeguard credible, transparent and peaceful elections in 2027

English: IEBC, CMD Engages Citizens at the 8th Peoples Dialogue Festival (PDF)4th Mar 2026. Today, Independent Electoral and Boundaries Commission (IEBC), led by Erastus Ethekon, addressed participants at the 8th People’s Dialogue Festival, held at Uhuru Park from 4th – 7th March 2026, reflecting on Kenya’s democratic challenges while expressing confidence in its continued progress. “It is both an honour and a responsibility to stand at Uhuru Park, a space deeply woven into Kenya’s democratic journey. Democracy is not sustained by institutions alone. It is sustained by participation, by trust, and above all, by people especially our youth,” said Ethekon. Erastus Ethekon underscored the urgency on boundary delimitation, matter, calling for structured and inclusive dialogue anchored in constitutional and legal frameworks. While acknowledging that the courts may pronounce themselves on specific issues, he emphasized that sustainable solutions require consensus-building and public confidence through open engagement. Turning to campaign financing and the cost of elections, he spoke frankly about the financial realities of administering credible, transparent, and verifiable elections. However, he cautioned that beyond administrative expenses, the escalating cost of political campaigns poses a deeper democratic risk. “Excessive and unregulated spending breeds inequality and creates fertile ground for malpractice,” he noted. Ethekon called for stronger transparency and accountability mechanisms. Addressing recent incidents of violence during by-elections, he firmly rejected the notion that intimidation equates to democratic participation. “We have witnessed disturbing scenes individuals armed with crude weapons, allegedly in the name of protecting their democratic rights. That is not democracy,” he stated. “ He said democracy must be safeguarded through institutions, dialogue, and respect for the rule of law not through violence. With the launch of a nationwide enhanced continuous voter registration exercise on 30th March 2026, the Chairperson placed particular focus on young Kenyans. He expressed confidence in their judgment, energy, and collective strength, reminding them that their power lies in their numbers. “You do not need any more power than that,” he said. “Register. Participate. This is not merely a right it is a civic duty and responsibility.” On security and peace, he was unequivocal: credible elections cannot take place in an environment devoid of stability. He challenged stakeholders present to move beyond rhetoric and ask the hard questions about how to create and safeguard a peaceful electoral environment. “That is the honest, forward-looking dialogue we must continue to have,” he remarked. Reflecting on the Commission’s renewed direction, the Chairman described the current IEBC as representing a paradigm shift. He observed that, unlike in the past when many citizens only became familiar with electoral leaders at the point of results declaration, the Commission has deliberately chosen openness from the outset. Since assuming office, the leadership has engaged youth in Kirinyaga, Machakos, and Nairobi, met with media, civil society, political parties, and development partners many present at the Festival. “We are fostering a culture of accessibility and transparency,” he said. “We are committed to being visible, accessible, and accountable.” He further proposed that forums such as the People’s Dialogue Festival be extended to counties across the country, with the Commission actively participating to dismantle outdated narratives that portray it as distant or opaque. “That narrative must become a thing of the past,” he affirmed. He pledged that the Commission would plan early, communicate early, and engage consistently. “We will explain ourselves clearly. We will tell our story every step of the way. That is our commitment to you especially to the young people of this country.” At the same time, he emphasized that elections cannot be delivered by one institution alone. The Commission will depend on collaboration with development partners, sister commissions, political parties, civil society, universities, colleges, and citizens at large. “Elections are a collective responsibility. We must all be involved. We must all be accountable. And together, we must safeguard our democracy.” In closing, the Chairperson urged Kenyans not to allow negativity to eclipse progress. He described Kenya’s democracy as resilient and evolving not broken. He highlighted the country’s advanced voter register, consistent deployment of electoral technology since 2013, and robust legal framework as areas of regional and global recognition. International electoral bodies across Africa and Asia, he noted, frequently seek to learn from Kenya’s experience, benchmarking its systems and reforms. “So let us not dwell only on our shortcomings. Let us also acknowledge the tremendous reforms we have undertaken, the institutions we have built, and the resilience we have demonstrated as a nation. Our democracy is a work in progress, but it is a strong one, and together, we will continue perfecting it,” he concluded. #FormNiDialogue #YourVoteYourFuture #TalkwithIEBC #StopFakeNews

English: IEBC Holds Planning Meeting for Enhanced Continuous Voter Registration2nd Mar 2026. The Independent Electoral and Boundaries Commission (IEBC) led by Chairperson Erastus Ethekon is holding a planning meeting for the forthcoming Enhanced Continuous Voter Registration (ECVR). The meeting aims to provide strategic direction on the national rollout of the exercise; clarify roles, responsibilities and coordination frameworks between field officers and headquarters teams, and legal & procedural guidelines; identify operational risks and formulate appropriate mitigation measures; develop a monitoring, evaluation and reporting framework with clearly defined performance indicators and shape a unified public communication and stakeholder engagement strategy for the ECVR period. The planned EVCR will commence on 30th March 2026 across the country for 30 days. The target is 2.5 million new voter registrations during Phase One of the ECVR exercise. The Commission projects a register of at least 6.3 million new voters to hit its projected target of 28.5 million voters in for the 2027 General Election. “The ECVR is one of the initiatives of fulfilling a constitutional obligation. Our fundamental objective is to ensure that every eligible Kenyan citizen can exercise their right to vote. The credibility of any electoral process begins with an inclusive, accurate and trusted Register of Voter,” said Ethekon. Further, the Chairperson observed that voter registration is a constitutional guarantee. Our responsibility is to make this exercise practical and accessible to all. IEBC is shifting from a passive model to a proactive one. By engaging temporary voter registration clerks, the Commission is deliberately bringing voter registration services to the people. The personnel will travel from village to village delivering registration services directly to the people. “Registration will be decentralized to the lowest feasible administrative levels and must also direct special attention and resources to remote, marginalized and hard-to-reach areas. Our approach must be adaptive to geographical and infrastructural challenges. No Kenyan should be excluded because of where they live,” said Ethekon. The Chairperson concluded by observing that ECVR exercise must be transparent, accountable and conducted with the highest standards of professionalism from recruitment of clerks and logistics until the data uploads of new enrollments. All personnel involved in the ECVR exercise must uphold the highest standards of integrity. “We are trustees of public confidence. Every action we take must reflect that responsibility,” Ethekon noted. Commissioner Dr Ann Nderitu, CBS, the Chairperson, Electoral Operations Committee said the target of 2.5 million voters over the next 30 days is grounded on demographic realities, particularly the large cohort of youth who have attained voting age since the last mass registration cycle. The credibility and inclusiveness of the 2027 electoral process will depend significantly on the Register we build today. She noted that the success of ECVR rests on three interdependent pillars; training, logistics and stakeholder engagement where emphasis will be placed on practical competency particularly biometric capture quality, kit operation, data transmission and troubleshooting in low-connectivity environments. Commissioner Nderitu urged that there should be strict adherence to the kit movement schedule to ensure timely rotation across wards and centres within the limited timeframe and real-time monitoring, rapid issue resolution and strong field supervision will be essential throughout the exercise. Ag. Commission Secretary/CEO Moses Sunkuli, OGW said ECVR will base its foundation on active network connectivity, logistic and compliance to data protection laws and urged staff to plan well by identifying the risks, challenges, and propose solutions going forward. “The Commission needs to ensure that network connectivity is up and running and any challenges still remaining are dealt with and given priority so that all our process and activities are supported by the network to make sure transfers and voter registration is real time. “From our past challenges, you are encouraged to come up with strategies that are accurate and consistent for registration of data. The voter education strategies must be purposefully designed to make sure all voters are educated and @IEBCKenya is able to receive interractive feedback. Lets go all out to engage and ensure all people participate,” Sunkuli said

The aim of the visit was for PSC to learn from the Commission’s experience, challenges encountered, and best practices applied in implementing the accrual-based framework, particularly on how the Commission adopted the inventory management system in support of IPSAS Accrual accounting. During the engagement, the Commission shared its experience in the implementation of the IPSAS Accrual Basis of Accounting, which it successfully adopted in the 2011/2012 financial year. CPA Nyakira noted that the adoption of the IPSAS Accrual Basis of Accounting enhances accountability, transparency, and openness in reporting on the use of public resources, while also providing a more comprehensive view of an institution’s financial position and performance. The PSC team, led by Mr. Martin Mokabi, Head of the Supply Chain Management Unit, and CPA Collins Adika, expressed appreciation to the Commission’s leadership for the opportunity to benchmark. The team is expected to fast-track the refinement and submission of the legislative instruments to Parliament in good time before the 2027 General Election. English: Press release - Collaboration with State Agencies on Managing the Register of Voters16th Feb 2026. Nairobi, Kenya: 16th February 2026 The Commission notes with concern recent statements by Democratic Party (DP) regarding IEBC’s engagement with National Registration Bureau in relation to voter registration data and identity verification. Article 88(4) of the Constitution of Kenya and Sections 4 and 6 of the Elections Act, 2011 mandate the Commission to, among other functions, register voters, maintain an accurate and up-to-date register of voters and ensure the integrity and accuracy of the register. Further, Article 249(2)(b) of the Constitution guarantees the Commission’s independence and provides that constitutional commissions shall not be subject to direction or control by any person or authority. In fulfilling this constitutional and statutory mandate, the Commission requires to work with relevant government agencies that are the lawful custodians of lawful and relevant data to the execution of its mandate. This includes collaboration with the State Department for Immigration and Citizen Services to make registration of voters efficient and inclusive in line with our mandate. In particular, The National Registration Bureau: To verify national identity card details and eligibility of citizens during voter registration to ensure the accuracy of the register of voters. Civil Registration Services: To confirm death records for lawful removal of deceased persons from the register of voters. The Directorate of Immigration Services: To verify passport details, noting that a Kenyan passport is one of the statutory identification documents permissible for voter registration under Regulation 13 of the Elections (Registration of Voters) Regulations, 2012 and Registration of Kenyan citizens residing out of Kenya under Regulation 34. Public agencies routinely enter into controlled data-sharing arrangements with population registration authorities for lawful service delivery, verification, and integrity purposes. Similarly, regulated private institutions such as banks, insurance firms, and telecommunications companies interface with population databases strictly for identity verification, compliance, and fraud prevention, subject to applicable laws and oversight. Therefore, the Commission has been engaging the State Department for Immigration and Citizen Services on various areas of collaboration including establishing a secure Application Programming Interface (API) link with Integrated Population Registration System (IPRS) to ensure only legitimate ID and passport numbers are used. Once the engagements are complete, the Commission will inform the relevant stakeholders. Conclusion The register of voters remains exclusively under the custody and control of the Commission, as provided for under the Constitution and the Elections Act. IEBC reiterates that personal data of voters is safeguarded in strict compliance with The Constitution of Kenya; The Elections Act, 2011; The Elections (Registration of Voters) Regulations, 2012; and The Data Protection Act, 2019. The Commission calls upon all stakeholders and partners to continue supporting lawful processes aimed at strengthening the accuracy and integrity of the register of voters, which is a fundamental pillar of democratic elections. We urge stakeholders, especially the political actors, to refrain from uncorroborated, inflammatory and divisive statements that not only undermine the integrity of electoral processes, but also the independence of the Commission. IEBC remains open for any clarification on the electoral processes. ERASTUS EDUNG ETHEKON, HSC CHAIRPERSON, INDEPENDENT ELECTORAL AND BOUNDARIES COMMISSION (IEBC)

English: IEBC and LSK Strengthen Partnership to Safeguard Electoral Integrity16th Feb 2026. Today, the Law Society of Kenya (LSK), led by its President Faith Odhiambo, paid a courtesy call to the Independent Electoral and Boundaries Commission (IEBC) . The Commission led by Chairperson Erastus Ethekon welcomed the LSK delegation and underscored the importance of the engagement. IEBC Chairperson Erastus Ethekon, HSC noted that the LSK is a key institution within Kenya’s governance framework. He emphasized thatIEBC occupies a critical position in the country’s governance architecture, with a clear constitutional mandate to manage elections, referenda and boundary delimitation processes. He acknowledged the vital role LSK has played in advancing reforms in Kenya and stated that the Commission cannot effectively discharge its mandate without close collaboration with the Society. He observed that the meeting was particularly important for the new Commission as it seeks to strengthen partnerships and explore practical ways of supporting each another in delivering the respective mandates. The Chairperson further affirmed that the Commission welcomes constructive criticism. He stated that feedback that helps to improve processes, systems and the manner in which the Commission executes its public mandate is always encouraged. Addressing the LSK delegation, he reiterated the Commission’s openness to listen, learn and work together in moving the country forward. Following the by-elections, the Commission conducted a comprehensive post-election review involving stakeholders such as security agencies, political parties, candidates and civil society organizations inter alias. The review examined what worked well, identified areas that required improvement and generated lessons to inform future electoral processes. IEBC Chairperson Erastus Ethekon, HSC observed that the Commission also took note of concerns raised by stakeholders regarding the presence of gangs around polling areas, incidents of voter intimidation and harassment, electoral violence, and voter bribery. He noted that such acts are unlawful and undermine the integrity of the electoral process. While the Code of Conduct Enforcement Committee is mandated to address violations of the Electoral Code of Conduct, it can only take action upon receipt of a formal complaint. “The Commission therefore urges candidates, political parties, and members of the public to promptly report any breaches to enable appropriate action to be taken in accordance with the law, as it remains committed to ensuring peaceful, transparent, and credible elections,” he said. The Chairperson cautioned against rhetoric that undermines public confidence in the electoral body, stating: “If political leaders portray the Commission as compromised, their supporters may lose faith in the process and choose not to register or vote, believing that their participation is meaningless. We must therefore work together to support the Commission in delivering free, fair, inclusive, transparent and credible elections.” Faith Odhiambo, President of the Law Society of Kenya, expressed appreciation to the IEBC Chairperson and Commissioners for convening the meeting, noting the longstanding partnership between LSK and the Commission anchored on the rule of law and constitutionalism. She recalled that in the 2022GE, the Commission maintained an open door policy that allowed LSK to provide input on electoral laws and reforms, even under tight timelines and significant operational pressure. She reaffirmed LSK’s commitment to supporting necessary legal reforms, including campaign financing laws, to enhance the integrity and smooth conduct of elections. Odhiambo emphasized that sustained stakeholder support is essential to strengthening Kenya’s electoral processes. On judicial engagement, she called for closer collaboration between the Commission and the Judiciary to minimize last minute court orders that often disrupt electoral timelines and create uncertainty for candidates and voters. Odhiambo further proposed joint Continuing Professional Development (CPD) sessions to enhance electoral knowledge among advocates, particularly young lawyers. She underscored the importance of broader public awareness through radio, observing that while Gen Z is active on social media, a significant portion of Kenyans still rely on traditional media platforms for information. In this regard, she noted that LSK plans to conduct nationwide civic education in September and October through LSK Legal Awareness Week, including the distribution of pamphlets covering key topics to be agreed upon with the Commission. "On the issue of disinformation, we must invest significantly in media monitoring and rapid response, especially to tackle AI-generated and manipulated content that disproportionately targets female candidates. Structured engagement with digital platforms is crucial to ensure swift action against users spreading harmful content," said Odhiambo. She concluded by emphasizing the continued partnership between LSK and the Commission in areas including election observation, accreditation, and electoral reform. #26thFebByelections | #YourVoteYourFuture | #TalkwithIEBC | #StopFakeNews

English: IEBC Joins KBC in Celebrating World Radio Day, Urges Youth to Register and Participate in Elections11th Feb 2026. The Commission today joined KBC to celebrate World Radio Day at their HQ in Nairobi. World Radio Day is a globally recognized event aimed at celebrating radio broadcast, improve international cooperation among radio broadcasters and encourage decision-making. The Commission was represented by Commissioner Dr. Alutalala Mukhwana, Chair of the Voter Education, Partnerships, Communications, and Stakeholder Engagement Committee (VEPSEC), who delivered a keynote speech on the importance of radio in election management. In his address, Commissioner Mukhwana emphasized that radio remains the most accessible and trusted medium for reaching citizens across the country, particularly young people, marginalized communities, and those in remote areas. He noted that radio continues to play a central role in voter education, civic awareness, and the dissemination of accurate electoral information. The Commissioner used the platform to urge young Kenyans to actively participate in the electoral process by registering as voters and turning out to vote when elections are held. He observed that youth participation in voter registration remains low, despite young people constituting a significant proportion of the country’s population. “While technology continues to evolve, citizens must use the systems available today to shape their future. We should not delay participation while waiting for future innovations,” Commissioner Dr Alutalala said. He addressed concerns raised by some young people who perceive the current voting system as outdated, clarifying that electoral participation should not be hindered by the absence of mobile or phone-based voting. Drawing parallels with the evolution of radio and music technology, he noted that meaningful progress is achieved by making the best use of existing tools. Commissioner Dr Alutalala informed participants that IEBC will roll out an enhanced voter registration exercise in March across the country. The exercise will ensure services reach communities at the grassroots level. He further dismissed claims that elections can be easily manipulated, stating that the Commission has put in place robust voter identification and verification measures, including the use of national identity cards, biometric fingerprint verification, and iris recognition. “The voting procedures currently in place makes it impossible for an unregistered person to vote. The system is secure and designed to protect the integrity of the electoral process,” he said. Commissioner Dr Alutalala assured Kenyans that the 2027 General Election will be peaceful, free, fair and credible, and encouraged all eligible citizens to register and vote in order to actively participate in determining the country’s future. The Commissioner was taken through the history of radio from 1927 to the present day, highlighting key milestones and technological advancements that have transformed radio broadcasting over the years. The presentation underscored how innovations in technology have expanded radio’s reach, improved content delivery, and enhanced its continued relevance in an evolving media landscape

English: IEBC and Nation Media Group Discuss Collaboration on Responsible Electoral Reporting5th Feb 2026. Today, Nation Media Group led by its Group Managing Director and Chief Executive Officer (CEO), Mr. Geoffrey Odundo, paid a courtesy call to the Independent Electoral and Boundaries Commission(IEBC) to discuss areas of collaboration ahead of the 2027 General Election. Speaking during the engagement, IEBC Chairperson Erastus Ethekon , emphasized the importance of responsible electoral communication, noting that while transparency and public-interest reporting are essential, messaging must be handled carefully to maintain public trust and participation. “As a public institution, we do not shy away from reporting legitimate issues. However, the framing and amplification of certain matters can sometimes unintentionally discourage voter participation or weaken confidence in the electoral process,” said Ethekon. The Chairperson highlighted challenges in mobilising resources for voter education and peace campaigns, observing that perceptions of adequate funding often limit support for critical communication initiatives. “To deliver a peaceful and credible election, we must invest deliberately in voter education and peace building. He emphasized that preparedness does not occur in isolation, noting that the Commission continues to engage faith-based organizations, civil society, political parties, media, security agencies, and development partners. These partnerships, he said, are critical to voter education, peacebuilding, transparency, and public trust. Despite progress, the Chairperson noted several challenges facing the Commission including inadequate and delayed funding, delays in electoral legal reforms, which ideally should be finalized at least one year before a General Election to allow effective preparation. Speaking on behalf of the faith community, EAK Chairperson Bishop Philip Kitoto noted that the Church’s mandate is to be salt in every sphere of society. He observed that Kenya, more than 50 years since independence, should not still be grappling with destructive vices, but instead should be modeling cohesion, integrity, and justice. The Prayer Breakfast provided a platform to reaffirm the role of faith leaders as trusted voices in society, particularly in promoting peaceful participation, ethical leadership, and national cohesion. They are deeply informed, digitally connected, and politically alert. If we engage them correctly, they become our greatest asset. If we fail, they could become a powerful source of instability,” said Dr. Alutalala Mukhwana. Mukwanja further pointed to the changing nature of the Kenyan voter, particularly young people, describing them as highly connected, politically alert, skeptical of traditional narratives, and quick to mobilise. English: Trust in election and why IEBC needs to enhance credibility in run up to 2027 GE 1113th Dec 2025. A month ago, Maurine Ochieng, the Commission Assistant Elections Officer (AEO) for Kisumu Central, sat in a community hall during the Citizens Election Watch forum pondering when did the wind change direction so fast. The air was thick with questions, some polite, some sharp. People spoke of “secret” biometric data, of agents barred from doing their duty, of a commission they felt was distant. But this was no protest. Officials from the IEBC sat at the front, not behind a distant podium. This was their strategy, to feel first hand, the perception gap on the Commission and its operations, years ahead of the 2027 General Election. The dialogue cut through noise with facts. • On Technology: “Is IRIS a spy tool?” A clear answer: No. It’s a legal identifier, like a fingerprint, governed by public regulations. • On Transparency: “Can agents photograph results?” Yes. Photographing Form 34A is not just allowed; it’s a safeguard. • On Integrity: “What about corruption in hiring?” The condemnation was absolute, backed by the weight of Chapter Six of the Constitution. The participants didn’t just state policies, they shared the data driving them, like the precise tally of new voter registrations in Kisumu County. Each number was a brick in a wall of credibility. From the talk, two salient recommendations were voiced. That the Commission must tell its own story.” Waiting for the final election report is too late. Continuous, proactive narrative-building is now a core part of electoral security. Secondly, the Commission must train observers adequately on the electoral process. Untrained observers, even well-meaning ones, breed misinformation. Joint training with the IEBC and other stakeholders creates a shared understanding of the process, turning watchdogs into informed partners. The Bottom Line The forum’s power wasn’t in solving every problem that day. Trust isn’t declared after a perfect election; it is built, transaction by transaction, in rooms like that hall. The lesson for 2027 is clear: integrity is built not just by running the vote, but by openly, and early, building the trust to make it credible

English: IEBC condemns violence and disruption of voting process witnessed during byelections in Kasipul, Mbeere and Malava6th Dec 2025. The Commission noted with grave concern the incidents of violence, intimidation, and disruption reported in parts of the country during the 27th November, 2025 by-elections and condemned in the strongest terms possible the acts of violence, hooliganism and lawlessness experienced in some electoral areas. We are working closely with security agencies to ensure swift action against any perpetrators. It is important that all political actors must uphold the principles of peaceful participation and respect for the rule of law,” said Ethekon. During the just concluded by-election, the percentage of voter turnout by each the 5 constituencies and Baring’o county was commendable. The Chairperson urged the voters to come out in large numbers to vote noting that their vote was their voice and that participation in the polling process strengthens Kenya’s democracy and every ballot contributes to a transparent and credible outcome. The Commission also pronounced itself on misinformation that circulated claims alleging ballot stuffing in some polling stations. “These claims are false, unfounded, and intended to mislead the public. All polling stations operated under strict procedures that included the presence of agents from participating political parties, accredited observers and security personnel. Every ballot issued corresponded to a verified voter, and all processes remained open to scrutiny. “The public should always rely on official communication from the Commission and refrain from sharing unverified information that would undermine public confidence in the electoral process. The Commission remains committed to delivering a transparent, peaceful, and credible by-election. I thank all voters, officials, agents, and observers for their continued cooperation. Violence and intimidation have no place in our democracy. We call on security agencies to act firmly where breaches occur

English: Commission highlights strategies to empower women in politics during mental health and inclusion forum11th Nov 2025. The Commission joined the Centre for Multiparty Democracy Kenya (CMD-Kenya), in partnership with Six Political parties to a round table discussion to explore the intersection between political participation, emotional wellbeing and gender inclusion. The forum themed “A Mental Health Approach to Women’s Political Participation” was held on 29th October 2025, at Kingfisher Nest Hotel in Nairobi and it brought together participants from CMD-Kenya, IEBC, Office of the Registrar of Political Parties (ORPP) and select political parties. Joyce Ekuam, the Ag. Director of Voter Education, Partnership and Communications, representing the Commission Secretary and CEO Marjan Hussein Marjan, explored IEBC sustained efforts to enhance women’s participation in politics. The presentation addressed the legal provisions on special interest groups, the IEBC’s constitutional and institutional mandate and the persistent challenges Kenyan women face in seeking elective positions. IEBC highlighted the legal framework that governs elections in Kenya and emphasized the initiatives to promote women’s leadership through voter education, stakeholder engagement and inclusive electoral processes. It also touched on the Commission’s constitutional mandate to support special interest groups. Ekuam further addressed the persistent challenges Kenyan women face in seeking elective office. Specifically, the Commission has made deliberate efforts to intervene and promote women participation in elections including development and implementation of a dedicated Gender and Social Inclusion Policy, reduced nomination fees for women candidates and enforcement of the two-thirds gender rule by rejecting non-compliant party lists. In addition, the Commission has established Women, Youth and Disability Inclusion Coordination Committees to enhance women participation in elections. Other interventions implemented include deploying an Electoral Risk Mapping Tool to identify and mitigate gender-based and cyber violence against women and strict enforcement of the Electoral Code of Conduct to penalize political malpractice. Beyond policy, the IEBC works to make electoral processes practically inclusive. This involves accrediting women-led organizations as voter educators and observers, granting priority voting to expectant mothers and using gender-sensitive messaging in voter education campaigns. “Partnerships with organizations like FIDA-Kenya strengthen these efforts, supported by vibrant IEBC Communication Centres to monitor and respond to electoral gender-based violence. The Commission also has a gender-sensitive budget policy to ensures funds are allocated for these critical initiatives,” said Ekuam. The presentation also recognized financial mechanisms that support women’s leadership, such as the Women Enterprise Fund, the National Government Affirmative Action Fund (NGAAF) and the Political Parties Fund. English: Commission engages State Department for Diaspora Affairs, explores ways to enhance voting for citizens living outside Kenya11th Nov 2025. Reflecting on past diaspora voter registration initiatives, Commissioner Ann noted that despite significant financial investment, the outcomes remained limited. She challenged the team to focus on innovation, efficiency, and value for money. “We need to find better, smarter ways to ensure that Kenyans abroad are effectively registered and able to vote, without incurring unsustainable costs,” she said. The State Department for Diaspora Affairs team was led by Mr. Edwin Limo, Director of Liaison and Partnerships. He reaffirmed the Department’s commitment to working with the Commission to ensure eligible Kenyans abroad are registered and able to vote as required by the Constitution

English: Ethiopian Civil Society Organisations for Elections tours IEBC, studies strategies to promote womens participation in polls6th Nov 2025. The Independent Electoral and Boundaries Commission (IEBC), led by Vice Chairperson Fahima Araphat Abdallah, OGW, hosted a delegation from the Coalition of Ethiopian Civil Society Organizations for Elections (CECOE) under the National Election Board of Ethiopia (NEBE) who are in the country for a study visit on strategies the Commission deploys to promote women’s participation in the electoral processes. The Vice Chairperson noted that even though Kenya has made progress in enhancing inclusion, participation of women in the electoral process is still a matter of concern, as they remain underrepresented. “There is need for targeted interventions to attain minimum requirements of gender equity to promote political representation,” she said. The Commission has put in place supportive legal and institutional structures, but women still face challenges in attaining equal participation and representation in Kenya due to societal contextual/cultural, religious factors, formal and informal rules and norms/gender roles. The Commission has made significant strides towards promoting the political participation of women, not only as voters, but also as candidates through development and implementation of a gender and social inclusion policy, cut down to half the nomination fees for women compared to other categories, rejected Party nomination lists that are not compliant with two-third gender rule. Further, the Commission has a Code of Conduct Enforcement Committee to hear, determine, and penalize candidates and political parties that perpetrate electoral malpractice: violence, intimidation, discrimination and destruction of campaign materials and gender rule. The Vice Chairperson said the Commission has also established Women Coordination Committees (WCC) that has national and grass-root levels which bring together women-led and women serving organizations from across the country to supplement the Commission’s outreach and advocacy efforts. This is besides deploying an Electoral Risk Mapping tool to enable identification of early signs of electoral violence including gender-based violence, cyber violence against women and girls. Abera Hailemariam, the Executive Director CECOE, said that the delegation seeks to strengthen the knowledge, skills, and strategies used by Kenya to advance women’s political participation. The mission will also promote regional peer learning and networking to encourage cross-country collaboration and exchange of innovative approaches

English: Commission resumes Continuous Voter Registration with colourful launch at Mashuuru Primary School in Kajiado19th Oct 2025. English: Commission engages Diaspora Affairs to enhance participation of citizens residing outside Kenya in elections29th Sep 2025. The Commission, led by Vice Chairperson Fahima Araphat Abdallah, OGW, held a consultative meeting last week with Roseline Njogu, CBS, Principal Secretary, State Department for Diaspora Affairs (SSDA) on modalities to enhance Kenya’s participation in the Diaspora Election processes. Ms. Fahima, representing the Chairperson Erastus Edung Ethekon, acknowledged that Kenyans in diaspora are a valuable national asset, who must be involved in the nation’s democratic and governance process. “They contribute socially, economically and politically to the country. With over one million Kenyans living abroad, diaspora remittances now standing at Ksh 6.5 billions, rank among the top sources of foreign exchange. Therefore, engaging them in national processes, including elections, is both strategic and essential,” said the Vice Chairperson. The Constitution of Kenya and Elections Act of 2011 provide for the progressive realization of voting rights for citizens residing outside Kenya. Since 2013, The Commission has facilitated diaspora participation in Presidential elections in accordance with these legal provisions. The Vice Chairperson further highlighted that in 2022, the Commission facilitated voting in 12 countries including Burundi, Rwanda, Tanzania, Uganda, South Sudan, South Africa, the USA, Canada, the United Kingdom, Germany, the United Arab Emirates (UAE) and Qatar. In the run up to the 2022 General Election, the Commission had a total of 10,443 registered voters in Diaspora. “The Commission faces significant challenges despite these achievements in implementing the Diaspora Election process, including low voter registration numbers, operational and logistical limitations, legal and policy constraints, limited awareness and voter education, and the perception of tokenism,” said Ms Fahima. The Principal Secretary stated that the State Department for Diaspora Affairs is committed to enhancing the participation of Kenyans abroad in the democratic process. Commissioner Dr. Alutalala Mukhwana, the Chairperson of the Voter Education, Partnerships, Stakeholder Engagement and Communications Committee, stressed that citizens living outside Kenya have every right to participate in elections. “The Commission is committed to finding ways to facilitate this participation and is seeking a collaborative partnership with SDDA to identify existing gaps and develop data-driven strategies that will ensure the diaspora’s participation in elections,” said Dr Alutalala. Marjan Hussein Marjan, MBS, the Commission Secretary/CEO, added that the Commission will continue to enhance diaspora participation guided by the 2025 population estimates that puts 1.46 million Kenyans living abroad, with 629,688 registered with Kenya High Commissions, Embassies and consulates. “The Commission remains committed to expanding and strengthening diaspora participation guided by updated data and strategic partnerships. With reforms, expanded access and sustained collaboration, diaspora participation will continue to grow and strengthen Kenya’s democracy,” said Marjan

English: IEBC identifies, tutors Training of Trainers ahead of national launch of Continuous Voter Registration exercise19th Sep 2025. This is not a discretionary task; it is a constitutional and legal duty that we must execute with both urgency and excellence. This training was not merely a scheduled event but it represented a strategic investment in the credibility of Kenya’s democracy. He urged participants to uphold integrity. “Integrity is not a suggestion, it is a condition of service,” said Marjan. The CEO emphasized that every decision and action must reflect the highest standards of honesty, impartiality and professionalism, as public trust in this institution is earned and is a collective responsibility. The training workshop addressed all aspects of the CVR process, from operational procedures to the technical details of the new Kenya Integrated Election Management System’s (KIEMS) voter registration module. The approach targeted to ensure consistency and standardization of electoral operations across all levels and offices of the Commission. Additionally, it will facilitate a uniform application of electoral laws, procedures, and technologies while enhancing preparedness and risk management for the CVR exercise. This training program is designed for both field Registration Officers and headquarters staff. The Master Trainers, responsible for developing the training content, will act as the lead trainers for the (ToTs) program. Afterwards, the ToTs will train registration officers in the to prepare for the resumption of the CVR exercise. The objective is to ensure that all levels of the Commission are fully equipped and ready for the start of the Continuous Voter Registration (CVR) process
